script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Hi, I’d like to join the centre. My name’s Daniel.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Thanks. Are you joining on your own?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: No, it’ll be a family membership: my wife and our two children.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: And what would you mainly use the centre for?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Swimming, mostly, and badminton at weekends.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: When would you like to start?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: The first of March is too soon, so let’s say the fourteenth of March.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Fine. The family rate is thirty-eight pounds a month.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Can we park at the centre?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, but you’ll need a permit from reception. It’s free for members.

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Can I ask how you heard about us?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: A friend of mine swims here and said it was great, so that’s really why.

answer.highlight: A friend of mine swims here and said it was great

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Good to hear. The pool does get busy, though, especially in the evenings after six.

answer.highlight: especially in the evenings after six

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Thanks. We’ll try to come earlier, then.

reading-1.title: Green Building Trends
reading-1.subtitle: How architects are rethinking the way buildings use energy and materials

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Green building refers to the practice of designing, constructing and operating structures in ways that reduce their impact on the environment across their entire life cycle. While early efforts in the 1970s focused narrowly on cutting energy bills after the oil crisis, the movement has since broadened to include water use, material sourcing and the health of the people inside.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Energy efficiency nevertheless remains the primary objective for most architects. Heating and cooling account for the largest share of a typical building’s energy demand, so designers concentrate first on the building envelope: the walls, roof and windows that separate inside from outside. High-performance insulation and triple glazing can sharply reduce heating requirements in cold climates.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Orientation is a cheaper but often overlooked tool. A building whose longest wall faces the sun can capture winter warmth through its windows, while overhanging roofs block the higher summer sun. Such passive design costs little to implement at the planning stage but is difficult and expensive to add later.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Materials have attracted growing attention. Concrete and steel carry a heavy embodied carbon cost, released during their manufacture long before a building opens. Some architects are turning to engineered timber, which stores carbon rather than emitting it, although critics question whether forests could supply enough wood if the practice became widespread.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Certification schemes have helped turn these ideas into market value. Buildings that meet recognised green standards often command higher rents, and in several cities public projects must now achieve a minimum rating. Yet some researchers warn that a certificate measures design intentions, not actual performance once the building is occupied.
